parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a sports centre to ask about membership.
script: Good morning, Riverside Community Sports Centre, Lucy speaking. How can I help?
Hi, yes. I've just moved to the area and I'm interested in joining the centre. Could you tell me about membership?
Of course. I can take some details first and then explain the options. Could I have your name, please?
Is that Harper with an E, H-A-R-P-E-R?
TN8 4RD. Lovely. And a contact number?

07739 516204. Great. Now, we have three types of membership. Full membership lets you use the gym, the pool and all classes at any time, and that's 36 pounds a month. Then there's off-peak, which is the same facilities but only before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends.
I work shifts, so I'm usually free in the daytime. How much is off-peak?
Off-peak is 24 pounds 50 a month. And there's also a swim-only option at 19 pounds.
I'd like to use the gym as well, so I'll go for off-peak.
Good choice. Are you interested in any of our classes? They're included in the membership.
I was thinking about yoga. Is there a yoga class on Thursdays?
There is, but I'm afraid the Thursday yoga class is full at the moment. There's a pilates class on Thursdays at the same time, though, and that has spaces.
Pilates is fine. I've done a bit before. Put me down for that.
Done. Now, when you come in for the first time, you'll need to bring proof of address, which you can show on your phone, and a photo for your membership card.

Yes, any recent photo of that size is fine. We'll also book you an induction session with one of our trainers, so they can show you how to use the gym equipment safely. Is the 21st of November any good?
I'm working on the 21st. What about later that week?
Great. And just for our records, how did you hear about us? Was it our website?
No, actually, a colleague at work recommended you. She comes here for swimming.
That's nice to hear. Well, that's everything, Mr Harper. We'll see you on the 23rd.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A librarian welcomes visitors on the reopening day of a town library.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the reopening of Marlow Central Library. My name is Grace Okafor and I'm the senior librarian here. I'd like to tell you a little about what has changed and then explain where everything is.

As many of you know, the library has been closed for some time. The original plan was to close for six months, but in the end the work took nine months, mainly because of problems with the old roof. Thank you all for your patience.

People often ask why we needed such a big renovation. We did reduce our energy costs with new windows and lighting, and we've made room for more books, but the main aim of the project was to make the building accessible. Before, wheelchair users simply could not reach the upper floors. Now there are two lifts and step-free entrances on both sides of the building.

Everyone will receive a new membership card today. You can still use it to borrow books and e-books, as before, but the new feature is that you can top it up with money and use it to pay for printing and photocopying. Unfortunately, the study rooms are still only open during our normal hours.
For families: children's story time used to be on Wednesday afternoons, but many parents told us that was difficult because of school pick-up, so it has moved to Saturday mornings at ten.

We are always grateful for volunteers. Our home delivery service for people who can't leave the house already has plenty of helpers, and our reading groups are run by members themselves. What we really need now is people to help visitors with computers, for example setting up email or filling in online forms.

Now, let me explain the layout. On the ground floor, near the main entrance, you'll find the information desk and new books. If you walk through to the garden side of the ground floor, that's where our new café is, with tables outside in summer.

Take the lift or stairs to the first floor. The east wing has the computer area, with twenty new machines. The west wing on the first floor is the new teen zone, which has its own games and study space for young people aged twelve to eighteen.
The second floor is now entirely a quiet study room. Please keep phones on silent up there.

Finally, the local history collection, including old maps and newspapers, has moved down to the basement, where we can control the temperature and humidity to protect the documents. You'll need to ask at the information desk to visit it. Right, does anyone have any questions?

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two college students, Maya and Tom, discuss their project on canteen food waste with their tutor, Dr Evans.
script: Come in, Maya, Tom. So, how is the food waste project going?
Quite well, I think. We've finished the survey of what gets thrown away in the canteen over two weeks.
And was there anything that surprised you?
Well, we expected a lot of vegetables to be wasted, and they were. But the really surprising thing was the bread. Almost a third of the bread rolls put out at lunch went in the bin.
And the staff weren't surprised at all. They already knew it was a problem, they just didn't have time to deal with it.
Interesting. You were going to survey students online as well, weren't you?
We started that way, but after a week only fifteen people had replied. So we switched to paper questionnaires on the tables in the canteen, and we got over two hundred.

Good decision. Now, I've looked at your draft presentation. The data is clear, and the charts are fine. What I'd like to see more of is practical solutions. At the moment you describe the problem very well, but you don't say much about what the college could actually do.

That makes sense. Actually, we spoke to the canteen manager last week. She wasn't keen on making portions smaller, because students complain. And she can't donate leftovers for health and safety reasons. But she did agree to try a system where students order their lunch in the morning, so the kitchen knows how much to prepare.
That's excellent, and it gives you a real solution to discuss. Let's meet again before you present. I'm busy on Monday and Wednesday. Would Friday work?
Friday's fine for both of us.
Good. Now, have you divided up the remaining work?

Mostly. I'm going to contact the local food bank, to ask what they do with donations from other organisations. And I'll do the analysis of the questionnaire data, since I'm more confident with spreadsheets.
I'll design the slides. And I want to interview two or three of the canteen staff, so we can include their views.
And the written summary for the report?
We'll write that together. It's probably best if we both agree on the wording.
Sounds like a good plan. See you on Friday.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture about urban heat islands.
script: Today I'm going to talk about urban heat islands: the reason why cities are often much warmer than the countryside around them, and what can be done about it.

Let's start with the causes. The first is the materials cities are built from. Dark surfaces, and asphalt in particular, absorb a great deal of the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly at night. Concrete and brick do the same, though to a lesser degree.

The second cause is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, trees and plants cool the air through evaporation and also provide shade. In dense city centres there is very little of this natural cooling.
Third, cities produce their own heat. Vehicles are a major source, and so are air conditioners, which ironically make the street outside hotter while they cool the inside of buildings.

So what are the effects? The difference is greatest at night. On a calm summer night, a city centre can be up to twelve degrees warmer than nearby rural areas. This leads to a sharp increase in electricity use, as people run fans and air conditioning for longer. The most serious effect, however, is on health. During heatwaves, the risk of illness and death rises, and elderly people are the most vulnerable, especially those who live alone.

Fortunately, there are solutions. One of the cheapest is the so-called cool roof. Roofs are painted white, or covered with a reflective material, so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. A step further is the green roof, which is covered with plants. Green roofs reduce temperatures and also absorb rainwater, which helps to prevent flooding.

Planting trees remains one of the most effective strategies, particularly along streets, where they shade both pedestrians and buildings. A well-known example comes from Medellín in Colombia. The city created a network of green corridors, planting trees and shrubs along roads and waterways. Within three years, temperatures in those areas fell by around two degrees. That may not sound like much, but during a heatwave it can make a real difference.

passages.title: Kerrigan Logistics: working from home policy
paras: Eligibility. Employees may apply to work from home once they have completed their six-month probation period. Working from home is limited to a maximum of two days per week, and managers may refuse requests where the role requires a physical presence.
How to apply. Requests must be made to your line manager using the online form on the staff portal. Email requests will not be accepted. You will normally receive a decision within ten working days.
Availability. Staff working from home may organise their own day, but they must be available by phone and video during core hours, which are 10 am to 3 pm.

Equipment and costs. The company will provide a laptop and a headset. Employees are responsible for their own internet connection, which must be fast enough for video calls. To help with heating and electricity, the company pays an allowance of £15 per month.
Health and safety. Before starting, you must complete a self-assessment checklist confirming that your workspace is safe, including your chair, desk height and lighting.
Data security. Laptops must be locked when not in use, and confidential documents must not be printed at home under any circumstances.

passages.title: Your first week at Brightwell Hospital: a guide for new staff
paras: A  A few days before you start, you will receive an email telling you when to collect your ID badge. Badges are issued at the security office next to the main reception. You will need the badge to enter staff areas, so please collect it before your first shift.

B  Your first day is an induction day. Everyone, whatever their role, must complete training in fire safety, infection control and the handling of patient information. You will not be allowed to start work on the wards until this has been signed off.

C  Staff in clinical roles are given two sets of uniform free of charge. Further sets can be ordered from the linen department. Uniforms must not be worn outside the hospital, except when travelling directly to and from work.

D  Staff parking is limited, and there is a waiting list for permits. We strongly encourage staff to use public transport: Brightwell staff receive a 30% discount on monthly bus passes, and there are secure bicycle shelters behind the main building.

E  The staff canteen on level 2 is open from 7 am to 8 pm, and staff receive a 20% discount on all meals. For those working at night, vending machines with hot food are available in the main corridor.
F  Starting a new job can be overwhelming. For your first month you will be paired with an experienced member of your team, known as a buddy, who can answer everyday questions and show you around.

G  Salaries are paid monthly, on the 28th. Payslips are not posted; you can view and download them through the online staff portal. Contact the payroll team if you have not received your login details by the end of your first week.

passages.title: The return of the night train
paras: A  For much of the twentieth century, overnight trains were a normal way to cross Europe. Passengers boarded in the evening, slept in a small cabin and woke up in another country. From the 1990s onwards, however, these services began to disappear. Budget airlines offered flights between major cities for less than the price of a sleeper ticket, and high-speed trains reduced daytime journey times so much that many routes no longer needed an overnight service. By 2015, several national rail companies had closed their night trains altogether, arguing that they were too expensive to run.

B  The decline was not inevitable, according to transport historian Lena Fischer. She points out that night trains were rarely marketed well and that the rolling stock, the carriages themselves, had often not been replaced for decades. 'Passengers were asked to pay more than an air fare to sleep in a cabin built in the 1970s,' she says. 'It is not surprising that they chose to fly.'

C  The turning point came in 2016, when Austrian Federal Railways decided to take over several routes that the German operator had abandoned. Under the brand name Nightjet, it invested in new carriages and introduced a wider range of tickets, from simple seats to private cabins with showers. Within a few years, many Nightjet routes were fully booked during holiday periods, and other operators, including several new private companies, began to plan services of their own.

D  Concern about climate change has been an important factor. A passenger travelling from Vienna to Brussels by night train produces only a small fraction of the carbon emissions of the same journey by air. Some governments have actively supported the revival. France, for example, has reopened two overnight routes from Paris with public funding, and the European Union has named night trains as part of its plans to reduce emissions from transport.

E  Yet the obstacles remain considerable. Each country has its own rail regulations, safety systems and electricity supply, so a train crossing several borders may need different locomotives and drivers along the way. Track access charges, the fees that operators pay to use the rails, can make up a large share of the ticket price. And because a carriage can only make one journey per night, night trains earn far less from each carriage than daytime services do. Industry analyst Marco Rossi believes that, without long-term public support, many routes will struggle to make a profit.

F  Passenger expectations are also changing. Surveys suggest that travellers are willing to pay more for a sustainable journey, but they also expect reliable wi-fi, good food and, above all, punctuality. A night train that arrives three hours late can ruin a business trip. Operators argue that if these expectations can be met, the night train could become not just a symbol of nostalgia, but a practical alternative to short-haul flights.
